domain: Design identity, governance, and monitoring solutions
summary: Architect Entra ID for identity, management groups/policy for governance, and Azure Monitor for observability as one unified control plane.
highYield: Hybrid identity sync choice: password hash sync (simple, cloud) vs pass-through auth (on-prem enforced) vs federation (ADFS/SAML, for SSO and advanced needs).
Entra External ID: B2B for partners (bring own identity) vs B2C for customers; Conditional Access + PIM for zero-trust least privilege.
Governance: management group hierarchy, Azure Policy + initiatives, resource locks, tags; policy enforces standards while RBAC enforces permissions.
Monitoring architecture: Log Analytics workspaces, Application Insights, alert rules + action groups, diagnostic settings.
Cost management: budgets, cost alerts, Azure Advisor, reservations and savings plans.
memoryAids: PHS = simple sync, PTA = on-prem enforced, Federation = ADFS/SAML SSO.
Policy = enforce standards; RBAC = enforce permissions.

summary: Select the right data store by workload type (relational, NoSQL, analytics) and design redundancy and tiering for durability and cost.
highYield: Relational: Azure SQL DB (DTU vs vCore, single/elastic/hyperscale) vs SQL Managed Instance vs SQL on VM (full control).
NoSQL: Cosmos DB - request units, partition keys, 5 consistency levels, multiple APIs (SQL, MongoDB, Cassandra, Gremlin, Table).
Analytics: Azure Synapse vs Fabric vs Data Lake Storage Gen2 (hierarchical namespace) and Databricks.
Storage: blob tiers (Hot/Cool/Cold/Archive), replication (LRS/ZRS/GRS/GZRS), lifecycle management.
Decision rules: transactional structured -> SQL; global multi-model low-latency -> Cosmos; big data/analytics -> Data Lake/Fabric.
memoryAids: Cosmos consistency: Strong, Bounded, Session, Consistent-prefix, Eventual.
RU = Request Units = throughput you pay for.
Hot data -> SQL/Cosmos; big data -> Data Lake; old data -> blob Archive.

summary: Design recovery around RTO and RPO using backup, replication, region pairs, and geo-redundancy to survive failures.
highYield: RTO (how long down) vs RPO (how much data lost) drive the BCDR design and technology choice.
Azure Backup (Recovery Services vault, point-in-time) vs Azure Site Recovery (continuous replication + failover to secondary region).
SQL HADR: Always On availability groups, auto-failover groups, and active geo-replication.
Geo-resilience: region pairs (max ~300 miles, sequenced updates), availability zones, GRS/GZRS storage, cross-region Front Door / Traffic Manager.
Failover testing and DR drills; storage account failover; App Service backups and snapshots.
memoryAids: RTO = how long down; RPO = how much data lost.
Backup = copy in time; Replication = copy in space.
Region pairs = ~300 miles apart, sequenced updates.

summary: Pick compute and network topologies (hub-spoke vs Virtual WAN) and a migration strategy that balances cost, performance, and security.
highYield: Compute selection: VMs vs VMSS vs App Service vs Functions vs AKS/Container Apps (control vs managed trade-off).
Network topologies: hub-spoke (central shared services) vs Azure Virtual WAN (global transit) vs mesh.
Connectivity: VPN Gateway vs ExpressRoute (bandwidth/latency/security); ExpressRoute SKUs (Local, Standard, Premium; Metered vs Unlimited).
Migration: Azure Migrate (discover/assess/migrate) and the 5 R's (Rehost, Refactor, Rearchitect, Rebuild, Replace).
Landing zones and the Azure Well-Architected Framework pillars (reliability, security, cost, operations, performance).
memoryAids: 5 R's = Rehost, Refactor, Rearchitect, Rebuild, Replace.
Hub-spoke = central shared services; VWAN = global transit.
ExpressRoute = private + predictable; VPN = encrypted over internet.
